title: Guards judge what actually runs
text: Every Bash guard reads one shared parse of the command, built once per hook call (`HookContext.shell`; the product-local subset builds the same parse once and hands it to each local policy). Heredoc bodies are input, not commands; statements split on unquoted `;`, `&&`, `||`, `&`, `|` and newlines before tokenizing, so a glued `;` never sticks to the previous word, while an operator inside `$(...)`, backticks, `<(...)` or `>(...)` belongs to that substitution, so `pytest $(find tests -name x.py | head -1)` stays one command; and a guard judges only the word in command position, after compound keywords, `NAME=value` assignments (including `_`-prefixed names) and an `env` prefix such as `env -i`. A quoted search pattern such as `rg 'a|pytest|b'` and a heredoc body fed to a typed `yoke` command are data, so neither is a writer or a `python -c` invocation; a body fed to a shell, or an unquoted body's substitutions, still runs and stays inspected. `git stash list` and `git stash show` are reads; other stash actions still change state. `yoke watch <kind>` with `--print-streaming-pair`, `-h` or `--help` before `--` only prints, so it needs no watcher timeout. The argv a direct `yoke qa mission host-command ... --` call ships runs on the Test Machine, so the path-claim guard does not fail closed on an `sh -c` there; a redirect or substitution still runs locally and stays enforced. Guards that need raw quote spans or fail-closed handling keep their own reading: path-claim parsing of expanding heredocs and redirects, the quoted function-payload guard, and the DB-command rule fragments that open `$(...)`. Observed in source and tests; deployed harness proof is pending.
